html:
A Portuguese fortress built at Malacca, on the west coast of the Malay peninsula, around 1512, right after the Portuguese captured the city. Only one gate, the Porta de Santiago, still stands.

Afonso de Albuquerque took Malacca from its sultan in 1511 and had the fort built at once, partly with stones taken from mosques and tombs. Its tall keep gave the whole fortress its name, "the famous one". For 130 years it guarded the Portuguese hold on the Strait of Malacca, the narrow sea lane between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea, and it beat off many attacks from Aceh and Johor.

In 1641 the Dutch East India Company and Johor took Malacca after a long siege, in the Battle of Malacca, and the Dutch rebuilt the walls. The British held Malacca during the Napoleonic Wars and began tearing the fort down in 1807 so no rival could use it. Stamford Raffles, visiting a few years later, is credited with saving the gate. See Portugal takes Malacca and the Malacca Sultanate that came before.
